newsitem.title: USA: Reno sees more deporations under U.S. immigration law.
newsitem.headline: Reno sees more deporations under U.S. immigration law.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said on Thursday a tough new U.S. immigration law that just took effect would lead to more deportations but not result in massive deportations.

At her weekly news briefing, Reno said the Justice Department would vigorously defend the law against various court challenges, including one by immigrant advocates over the procedures affecting asylum seekers at the border.
"What we want to try to do is to make sure that it is enforced fairly. We are committed to enforcing the law, but to ensuring that it is done so in a just and humane manner," she said.

"Our overwhelming efforts will be to focus on those individuals illegally in this country who have engaged in criminal activity. The new law will lead to more deportations, but there will be no massive deportations," she said.

All claims for relief under the law would be handled on a case-by-case basis, Reno said, adding the government wanted to enforce the law against illegal immigration consistent with the "principles of due process and fair play."
The law, approved by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton in September, has created widespread confusion in some communities with large immigrant populations.

The problems were compounded by a federal judge's ruling on Monday evening that briefly delayed the law's regulations. But a U.S. appeals court overturned the decision, allowing the law and the regulations to take effect on schedule on April 1.

The law's overall purpose was to tighten U.S. borders against illegal aliens by increasing the number of border patrol agents, improving technology and beefing up barriers along the U.S.-Mexican border.

Deportation procedures were streamlined under the law and the number of aliens exempted from deportation was capped. Foreigners ineligible to enter the United States now face "expedited removal" at ports of entry and immigrants who remain in the United States with expired visas and then leave are barred from returning for three to 10 years.
